title: Turn two hurdles round so their feet face the runners' approach
instruction: Set the hurdles for the race.
context: A hurdle stands on L-shaped feet that must point toward the runners' approach: a runner who clips the bar then tips the hurdle over away from them. Set the other way round, the feet brace it, it cannot fall, and the runner trips over it and crashes: a correctly set hurdle topples at a push of about 4 kg on its bar, while one set backwards takes many times that. World Athletics' technical rules require hurdles to be placed with the feet on the side from which athletes approach, and coaches and track officials check it before every race. Here both hurdles were put out the wrong way round on their marks, and the direction of running is shown by the starting blocks and the finish line. The instruction says only to set the hurdles. Done by: track officials, coaches and PE teachers.
setup: A red rubber track (50 x 44 cm) runs away from the arms, from 12 to 62 cm in front of the arm bases, with white lane lines making two lanes centred 11 cm left and right of centre. A white start line crosses it 16 cm out, with blue starting blocks just before it in each lane, and a black and white chequered finish line crosses it 58 cm out. In each lane a pair of yellow marks 34 cm out shows where its hurdle stands. Two hurdles (14 cm wide, 9 cm tall, 150 g): a white bar with black stripes on two black uprights, each upright on an L-shaped black foot 8 cm long. Both stand on their marks with their feet pointing toward the finish. Also: two cones, a stopwatch and a clipboard beyond the finish.
scoring: A hurdle is set when it stands upright (tilted less than 10 degrees) and at rest, its uprights within 3 cm of its marks, with its feet pointing back toward the start line within 30 degrees. 0.5 for each set hurdle. Scored at the end.
reset_notes: Stand each hurdle back on its marks with its feet pointing toward the finish line; nothing is consumed.
fidelity: A scale model: hurdles are rigid, a fifth of full size and much lighter, and no runner is simulated, so a clipped hurdle is never shown tipping. The scorer checks what an official checks before a race: each hurdle standing on its marks with its feet toward the approach.
